item.title: The struggle for freedom: How BSD escaped AT&T licensing
item.description:
16. BSD Unix, Part 6 - The Struggle for Freedom BSD Unix, Part 6 The Struggle for Freedom

Early Unix was available through inexpensive source-code licenses because a 1956 antitrust settlement kept AT&T out of the commercial computer business [6]. Some early licenses cost just $99 [1].

Too cheap.

One tape,please.

Schoolstoo?

Companiestoo?

Researchlabs too?

Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) also valued Unix's source-code availability. That was why it chose BSD Unix over DEC's VMS for building the Internet [1].

But AT&T's breakup in 1984 opened the way for it to sell Unix commercially. AT&T abruptly raised the price from $99 to $250,000 [1].

AT&T Unix fees

Khh...

BSD still required an AT&T license. When fees rose, some companies wanted its networking code separately.

How can I get just BSD'sTCP/IP and vi source code?

AT&T's raised the fees.Users want just ournetworking code and tools.

Let's release ournetworking codeand tools separately.

How's the releasecoming?

Fine. What aboutthe license?

Let's write our own BSDlicense. BSD users can useour code freely. They justneed to put the copyrightnotice in the manual ifthey make a product orredistribute the source.That'll throw AT&T off.

Anything goes, huh? Well, we don't want to putrestrictions on people like AT&T does.

CSRG released its networking code and utilities as Networking Release 1 (Net/1) in June 1989. Its new BSD license allowed use without an AT&T source license. People could modify the code or redistribute it as source or binaries without paying Berkeley royalties. They had to retain the source copyright notices and credit UC Berkeley and its contributors in product documentation.

BSD's networking releaseis finally here.

Howmuch?

They'll mail you a tapefor $1,000. Or download itfree by FTP. We can evenchange and redistributethe code without royalties.

 Meanwhile, at CSRG

Professor, the networkingrelease is selling well.

Grants, tape sales...Development's fundedfor a while.

Time for the weekly meeting.

Professor, why don't we make a version of BSDthat doesn't require an AT&T Unix license?

We can't keep depending on AT&T.We've already changed much of the kernel.It's the tools and C library we need to rewrite.Can we do it quickly?

Let's try. With help fromoutside contributors, we canrewrite the AT&T code.

CSRG decided to rewrite AT&T's tools and C library. With help from outside contributors, most of the code was rewritten in eighteen months.

With most of AT&T's Unix code removed, a completely free BSD Unix was finally released in June 1991. The source was still available on tape for the $1,000 copying fee, or as a free download by FTP.

Now we can sellBSD Unix too.

CSRG founded a company called BSDi to sell BSD Unix commercially. The University of California also began selling BSD Unix in the early 1990s. An advertisement claimed it was 95% cheaper than AT&T Unix. That did not go down well with AT&T.

The Empire Strikes Back

In April 1992, AT&T subsidiary USL sued BSDi. UC Berkeley was added to the lawsuit later.

I thought we'd removedall the AT&T code...What's this?

But AT&T's Unix System V also included plenty of BSD code, such as virtual memory, TCP/IP and vi. The BSD license allowed anyone to use the code if they kept the copyright notices. AT&T removed those notices from the source and sold Unix as though it had written all the code itself.

AT&T's suing us for distributingUnix code without permission.

That's absurd. System V includesour virtual memory, TCP/IPand vi code.

Exactly. We shouldcountersue.

The BSD side filed a countersuit against AT&T.

In February 1994, the two sides agreed that each could sell Unix, provided CSRG removed some remaining AT&T Unix code.

It's the same code...Wouldn't want his job.

Although BSD Unix began with AT&T's code, much of it had been rewritten, and evidence had emerged that AT&T had incorporated BSD's TCP/IP, virtual memory and vi code while removing copyright notices. But legal uncertainty hung over BSD distribution during the lawsuit, and the two years lost before a completely free BSD Unix appeared gave Linux room to grow.

If I could have installed BSD Unixon my Intel 386 PC,I wouldn't have needed to write Linux.

That wraps up our six-part story of BSD Unix!

References Andrew Leonard, BSD Unix: Power to the people, from the code, 2000 Marshall Kirk McKusick, Twenty Years of Berkeley Unix: From AT&T-Owned to Freely Redistributable, in Open Sources: Voices from the Open Source Revolution, O'Reilly, 1999 Computer Systems Research Group The Design and Implementation of the 4.4BSD Operating System: Network Implementation Mike Linksvayer, Interview with Linus Torvalds, Meta Magazine, 1993 Federal Judicial Center, The Breakup of "Ma Bell": United States v. AT&T Dennis Ritchie, Old Unix Licenses and Price Lists

GL.iNet Security Notice 2026-11-20

SECURITY NOTICE · CUSTOMER ADVISORY

GL.iNet Router and KVM Security Incident

Issued | Last updated

About the incident

On November 20, 2026, GL.iNet identified a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services. An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices.

The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. The cloud-side fix alone does not remove malware from devices that were already infected; install the security firmware below to remove it.

Download and install the security update

Install the latest stable security firmware for your exact model as soon as possible, even if the checks below find no signs of infection. The security firmware update removes the malware identified in this incident without requiring a factory reset. You can keep your existing settings during the update.

Router security firmware downloads GL-MG1300, GL-MT3000, GL-MT6000 (4.11.1 or later) GL-E5800 (4.10.3 or later) GL-BE3600, GL-BE9300 (4.10.2 or later) GL-BE14000 (4.9.3 or later) GL-BE6500, GL-MT3600BE, GL-MT5000 (4.9.1 or later) GL-BE10000 (4.8.7 or later) GL-AX1800, GL-AXT1800, GL-SFT1200, GL-X3000, GL-XE3000 (4.8.4 or later) GL-MT2500 / GL-MT2500A, GL-X2000 (4.7.14 or later)

If your router is not listed, check the GL.iNet Download Center or email support@gl-inet.com. Do not install firmware for another model. An unlisted model is not necessarily unaffected.

KVM security firmware downloads

If you installed a security beta, upgrade to the latest stable firmware for your model.

What you should do

Follow the steps below to check your device. For both routers and KVM devices, look for the exact text crond -i /tmp/.log within the details of a running process. The process entry may contain other information.

If you find the indicator: Treat your device as infected. Install the latest stable security firmware for your model using the download links above. You can keep your settings during the upgrade. If your model is not listed, the upgrade fails, or the indicator is still present after the upgrade, contact support@gl-inet.com for recovery guidance. If the check completes without finding the indicator: If you have no other reason to suspect infection, no factory reset or other cleanup is needed. The stable security update is still recommended. If you cannot complete the check or are unsure about the result: Contact support@gl-inet.com for help. How to check a GL.iNet router Option 1: Use the web admin panel (LuCI) In the router’s Admin Panel, go to System → Advanced Settings and sign in to LuCI. In LuCI, open Status → Processes. Press Ctrl+F (Command+F on macOS) and search for tmp/.log. Check whether a matching process shows crond -i /tmp/.log. Option 2: Use SSH

Sign in to your router via SSH and run the following command. If you are unfamiliar with SSH, please refer to our Router SSH Login Guide or contact our technical support team at support@gl-inet.com for assistance.

ps | grep tmp

Look for crond -i /tmp/.log in the output. A line showing only the grep command is not a match.

How to check a GL.iNet KVM

In the KVM web interface, go to Toolbox → Terminal → Access to open the device terminal. For step-by-step instructions on Comet Q (RMQ1), see the KVM Console Guide. Run the command for your model in the KVM’s terminal, not on the connected computer.

RMQ1:

ps -a | grep tmp

All other KVM models:

ps -aux | grep tmp

Look for crond -i /tmp/.log in the output. A line showing only the grep command is not a match.

If your KVM is infected, also check the connected computer

As a precaution, check for unfamiliar programs, browser extensions or user accounts; unexpected startup items or scheduled tasks; and unusual settings changes or network activity. Run a full scan with up-to-date security software.

Additional Security Check (Third-Party Tool)

As our investigation continues, additional indicators of compromise have been identified. The official quick checks described above may not detect every affected device.

Both checking approaches are available for GL.iNet routers and KVM devices: the official device-specific quick checks above and the optional third-party tool below. Follow the instructions appropriate for your device. The two approaches have different detection coverage, and neither can guarantee that a device is free of compromise.

For users who wish to perform a more comprehensive check, an independently developed community tool is available:

Community Security Check Tool (Unofficial)

Disclaimer: This is an independent third-party tool and is not developed, verified, maintained, endorsed, or supported by GL.iNet. GL.iNet does not control the tool's functionality, accuracy, security, availability, or data-handling practices, and cannot guarantee its results. Use of this tool is entirely optional and at the user's own discretion and risk. It is not part of GL.iNet's official support or remediation process.

Before using the tool, review its instructions and source code. It may run with administrative privileges and includes optional remediation, evidence-collection, and reporting functions. Users should evaluate those functions carefully before enabling them. The absence of findings does not guarantee that a device has never been compromised.

For official device recovery instructions and security firmware updates, please continue to follow GL.iNet's published guidance.

Firmware release, customer notifications, and investigation Firmware release: Stable security firmware is available for the router and KVM models listed above. Use the download link for your exact model. Customer notifications: We will notify customers we identify as affected by email at the address associated with their GL.iNet cloud account. These emails will include device-specific guidance. You do not need to wait for an email to check your device or install the update. Ongoing investigation: We are still determining the scope of the incident, including whether computers connected to affected KVM devices were impacted. We will update this notice as we confirm new information. Contact

For questions, please contact support@gl-inet.com.

To report a security issue, contact security@gl-inet.com.

We apologize for the concern this may cause and are committed to keeping you informed.

GL.iNet Security Team

About GL.iNet

Founded in 2010, GL.iNet is a leading provider of innovative routers and networking solutions. From compact travel routers to cutting-edge remote KVMs, GL.iNet delivers award-winning networking technology designed for performance and security.

GL.iNet gives people and organizations the power to connect with confidence. By putting control in the hands of users, GL.iNet supports the productivity and collaboration that shape a Good Life.

Treemap of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean Proof
item.description:
The Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, as a treemap

On 20 November 2026 Levent Alpöge released a Lean 4 formalization, written with Claude, that states and proves the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalization to Dirichlet L-functions. The source is 175,187 modules (a module is one .lean file). This page shows what is in them.

The statement

These two files are the whole claim. Statements.lean defines four propositions. Main.lean proves them, and Mathlib's own RiemannHypothesis, by citing theorems from the other 175,185 modules. Point at a symbol to see how to say it and what type it has.

In words: every zero of the Riemann zeta function, other than the trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, … , has real part ½. For every Dirichlet character χ, every zero of L(s, χ) with real part strictly between 0 and 1 has real part ½.

Map of every module

Each rectangle is one module. Modules are grouped by directory, and a larger rectangle means more of the chosen size measure.

Scroll over the map to zoom, drag to move, click a module to read its code.

Highlight modules that mention

Terms come from Alpöge's announcement and from standard number theory. A module is counted if the term's identifier appears in its text, not counting import lines.

Highlight a step of Alpöge's timeline

Where each step appears to live in the Lean code, according to a blueprint of the proof by GitHub user jae-63. ● found clearly ◐ names and position fit ○ weak evidence. The number is how many modules match. Point at a step to see it on the map; click to keep it highlighted.

What takes up the space By top-level library Why so many modules Areas of mathematics

Each module's field is predicted by a classifier from the Mathlib and project identifiers it uses. The prediction agrees with a language model's reading of the module about half the time (details under Sources and method). Point at a row to see where that field sits on the map.

The line under each field lists objects and theorems named in the labels that a language model gave to each of 746 directories after reading a digest of its identifiers. Treat them as a guide, not a census.

How modules depend on each other

A comment on Hacker News reported 204 modules "not referenced anywhere", without a list or a method. In the import graph no module is unreferenced: every module except Main.lean is imported by at least one other module. The comment may be counting something that imports do not show, such as declarations that nothing uses.

Import graph of the main directories

Scroll the graph sideways to see all of it.

Longest import chain Modules that the most other modules depend on Numbers and tactics

Colour the map by or by .

Modules with the largest share of digit characters Tactics used

Point at a bar to see what the tactic does and which modules use it.

Who has checked the proof

What each of these public pages reported when read on 23 November 2026. None of the checks were run in building this page.

The Lean statements cover the Riemann zeta function and Dirichlet L-functions. They do not cover Dedekind zeta functions or automorphic L-functions.

Sources and method The Lean source is from Alpöge's announcement. The page reads it from the mirror 1337isnot1337/riemann-hypothesis-solved at commit 6193bb5. The archive declares no licence, so this site does not store the Lean files; it stores module names and counts, and loads code from the mirror when you open a module. All counts on this page come from a script that reads every file once. Its totals match the independent checks above: 175,187 files, 17,374,215 lines, longest import chain 203. Declarations are counted by matching keywords such as theorem and def at the start of a line. Lean's kernel sees more declarations (1,484,729 in the nanoda runs) because Lean generates auxiliary ones. The proof steps on the map follow jae-63's blueprint, which matched Alpöge's timeline to Lean names by search and partial reading. It is one reader's interpretation.

item.title: The New Docker: Built to Run on Trust
item.description:
Evolving an iconic brand for the agentic era

Today, Docker is officially launching its new brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.

Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents?

That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a new Docker.

A new Docker, but a familiar story.

We’ve been here before

Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment.

Enter a company you might have heard of: Docker.

Together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.”

Today, of course, the challenge confronting us is new and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers.

What isn’t changing

Let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it.

The qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us.

On the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way.

Containers weren’t designed for agents

Agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.

Agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.

Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.

Run on trust

In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the new Docker is all about trust.

Trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.

Trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.

Trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this big alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.

Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.

A whale of an evolution

As our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a new day for Docker. Something that says and shows, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.

Something big.

Something, dare I say, whale sized.

I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.

If you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation company, Motto, we landed on a new Moby for the new Docker.

Watch Moby’s transformation here:

In many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a new era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.

Come take a look around

We’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our new website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.

Wherever this new era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

item.title: XNU Linux: Full OS X GUI Userspace on Linux
item.description:
Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it.

xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel module (xnu.ko) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module (fki.ko).

With a stock Ubuntu kernel, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome.

One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 (sw_vers, the Darwin kernel, launchd, WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu, Linux 7.0, the xnu and fki modules loaded, and the insmod xnu.ko process the macOS kernel runs in). Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800.

The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge).

Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on (GPU=auto).

macOS processes (launchd, WindowServer, Safari...) Linux processes (systemd, sshd, xnudrmd...) ────────────────────────────────────────────────── ──────────────────────────────────────────── XNU (source-built, LINUX64 machine layer, kexts) │ ↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h) xnu.ko (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection) ↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*) fki.ko (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls) Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC) CPUs: each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host (idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and fki.ko forwards the faults and user exceptions of XNU code to XNU's handlers. Memory: XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages). Devices: kexts in kexts/ give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge. GPU: Metal in the hosted macOS runs on gpu/xnu-cpu-metal (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux host's GPU through the DRM bridge (kexts/XnuDrm → host call → gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd → the Linux render node), using Mesa's Venus driver; without a GPU it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU.

Working, on an Apple Silicon Mac running an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit) with 1 to 6 hosted CPUs:

macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac: 49 s). Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes, Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report. Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each run's log kept in /var/log/xnulinux/. The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU (Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max)) and is enabled by default (GPU=auto) when a Linux render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering (GPU=off) otherwise.

What is still a stopgap is listed in docs/production.md. Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K).

An arm64 Linux host with PAC (Apple Silicon M1 or later in a VM: krunkit for GPU access, or tart), 4K pages, 16 GB of RAM (8 GB of it reserved for the hosted kernel). A Mac with Xcode to make the system disk and build the GPU parts. A macOS 27 installation (an Apple Virtualization VM disk) of your own. No Apple binaries are in this repository or distributed by it: the kexts Apple ships, the macOS system disk and its trust cache come from your own installation. scripts/vm-xnu-build.sh (in the Linux VM, once): sets up the macOS-DroidVM Linux toolchain and builds XNU (xnu-12377.121.6) natively on arm64. scripts/vm-xnu-rebuild.sh: applies xnu-patches/, builds the kernel and kexts/, and links the kernel collection with Apple's kexts from your macOS installation. scripts/mk-macvm-disk.sh (on the Mac): turns a macOS VM disk made by Apple's installer into the hosted system's disk and copies it into the Linux VM. scripts/xnulinux-boot.sh (in the Linux VM): builds fki.ko and xnu.ko against the running kernel, brings up the network (and the GPU bridge when there is a render node) and boots the hosted system. Its console is scripts/xnu-console.sh, its screen tools/hosted/fb2png.py, input tools/hosted/xnu-input.py. scripts/install-service.sh (in the Linux VM): runs it as xnulinux.service, configured in /etc/xnulinux.conf (CPUs, memory, disk, GPU). On the Mac, scripts/install-krun-agent.sh keeps the VM itself running. GPU (optional, on the Mac): gpu/venus/build-darwin.sh builds the hosted Vulkan driver, gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/ the Metal plugin (see its README).

The Linux side and the XNU side are kept apart by license and meet only at FKI. Every source file carries an SPDX-License-Identifier; the license texts are in LICENSES/.

Path License What fki-ko/, linux/ GPL-2.0-only FKI: the out-of-tree module for stock kernels, and the same as an in-tree driver xnu-ko/ APSL-2.0 xnu.ko: loads XNU's kernel collection and runs it; calls Linux only through fki_* xnu-patches/ APSL-2.0 The LINUX64 machine layer and the other changes to XNU's sources, and their shared headers kexts/ APSL-2.0 The hosted system's kexts (CPU, disk, keystore, Metal accelerator, DRM bridge) kexts/XnuDisplay/, kexts/XnuEthernet/, kexts/XnuInput/ BSD-2-Clause-Patent Derived from macOS-DroidVM's kexts gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/ GPL-2.0-or-later The Metal plugin over metal2vulkan (GPL-2.0-or-later); XnuCpuMetalShim.h is BSD-2-Clause-Patent (from AdrenoMetal) gpu/xnu-drm/ GPL-2.0-only, MIT xnudrmd (the Linux end of the DRM bridge) is GPL; the protocol header and darwin/ (built into Mesa) are MIT gpu/venus/ GPL-2.0-only; patches MIT Build scripts and tests; the patches to Mesa and virglrenderer are under their upstream license (MIT) gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/patches/ upstream's Patches to Mesa (MIT) and metal2vulkan (GPL-2.0-or-later) scripts/, tools/, tests/, docs/ GPL-2.0-only Build, disk, boot, debugging and test tools; documentation

xnu.ko is on the XNU side of the line: it runs XNU's code in its own address space, so it is APSL-2.0 like XNU, and Linux reports it as a non-GPL module (MODULE_LICENSE("Proprietary"), which taints the kernel as ZFS does). It must not include Linux headers beyond the module ABI, call Linux functions other than fki_*, or carry Linux code. Upstream code (XNU, macOS-DroidVM's toolchain, Mesa, metal2vulkan, the Vulkan loader, LLVM) is fetched at pinned revisions and patched at build time; it is never committed.

macOS-DroidVM and UniXNU: the 4K-page XNU base, the Linux-hosted XNU toolchain, and the display, Ethernet and input kexts these are derived from. metal2vulkan, Mesa (Venus, lavapipe), virglrenderer and krunkit. Apple's open-source XNU.

item.title: A Partial Evaluator for C
item.description:
Tempo Specializer - A Partial Evaluator for C What is Tempo? Partial evaluation is program transformation that automates a program specialization process. Tempo is a partial evaluator for C programs. It has been applied in various domains such as operating systems and networking, computer graphics, scientific computation, software engineering and domain specific languages. A first workshop on Tempo has been organized in March 1998. Tempo is now being distributed. Its documentation is available on line, as well as tutorial slides. An Overview of Tempo Tempo is a partial evaluator for C programs. It is being developed in the Compose project at IRISA / INRIA - LABRI (France).

Tempo is an off-line specializer; it is divided into two phases: analysis and specialization.

The input to the analysis phase consists of a program and a description of which inputs will be known during specialization and which will be unknown. Based on this knowledge, dependency analyses propagate information about known and unknown values throughout the code and produce an annotated program, indicating how each program construct should be transformed during specialization. Because C is an imperative language including pointers, the analysis phase performs alias and side-effect analyses in addition to binding-time analyses. The accuracy of these analyses is targeted towards keeping track of known values across procedures, data structures, and pointers.

Following the analysis phase, the specialization phase generates a specialized program based on the annotated program and the values of the known inputs. Tempo can specialize programs at compile time (i.e., source-to-source tranformation) as well as run time (i.e., run-time binary code generation).

For more details, please consider reading some of our papers, most of which are available at the following URL: papers. Program Analysis As a first step, the user provides a program and specifies what arguments (including global variables) are static. For example, the user provides the following code for a miniprintf function, and specifies in this way that the first argument is static whereas the second is dynamic: miniprintf(S,D). miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[]) {   int i = 0;   while( *fmt != '\0' ) {     if( *fmt != '%' )        putchar(*fmt);     else       switch(*++fmt) {         case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break;                      case '%' : putchar('%');     break;         default  : prterror(*fmt);   break;       }     fmt++;   } }From this Tempo produces a program file with analysis annotations. These annotations can be visualized using colors that highlight the propagation of the known/unknown information throughout the program./*  LEGEND:  STATIC  DYNAMIC  */ miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[]) {   int i = 0;   while( *fmt != '\0' ) {     if( *fmt != '%' )        putchar(*fmt);     else       switch(*++fmt) {         case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break;                       case '%' : putchar('%');     break;         default  : prterror(*fmt);   break;       }     fmt++;   } }The blue color (bold face for black and white display) represent static constructions, i.e. values that can be computed at specialization time. The red color (standard font for black and white display) is for dynamic expressions, whose value cannot be precomputed knowing only the static arguments. Basically, everything in blue (bold) will disappear after specialization; only red (standard font) parts will remain.

The visualization of the analysis is very important for the user to assess the amount of specialization in the code. Furthermore, the analysis speeds up the specialization process (as opposed to on-line partial evaluators). The analysis is inter-procedural and takes into account pointer aliases and side-effects.

Compile-Time Specialization When the user is satisfied with the analysis (i.e., what the user expects to specialize indeed appears as static), actual specialization values must be provided. For example, giving "<%d,%d>" as the actual specialization value for the fmt argument of the miniprintf() function yields the following specialized code. miniprintf_1(int val[]) {   putchar( '<'    );   putint ( val[0] );   putchar( ','    );   putint ( val[1] );   putchar( '>'    ); }Many specializations can be made, sharing the same analysis. Only different specialization values have to be provided. Runtime Specialization Tempo can also perform runtime specialization, using optimized binary code templates. A dedicated runtime specializer is generated from the analysis of the program. In the case of the miniprintf function, Tempo generates a runtime specializer rts_miniprintf_1() which can be used as in the following example. /* * Some dynamic execution context for variable 'format' */ spec_printf = rts_miniprintf_1(format); ... (*spec_printf)(val1); /* <=> miniprintf(format,val1) */ (*spec_printf)(val2); /* <=> miniprintf(format,val2) */The function rts_miniprintf_1() is a dedicated runtime specializer. It returns a pointer to the specialized function. Several specialized versions can also be generated and used at the same time. Applications of Tempo Tempo has been successfully applied in various domains, yielding substantial speedups. Operating system and networking: Sun RPC, Chorus IPC, BSD packet filter, Unix signals, active networks, Computer graphics (various filtering algorithms), Scientific computation (trajectory, FFT, math libraries), Software architectures and mechanisms: Domain specific languages GAL, PLAN-P), Selective broadcast (implicit invocation), Pattern matching, Interpreters, Software layers, Generic libraries.For an up-to-date list of non-confidential, published applications, please browse our ``papers'' web page: papers.

Besides C, Tempo is currently being used as a back-end for specializing Java programs using Harissa, a JavaVM-to-C compiler. Fortran and C++ programs have also been specialized using translators to C.

Projects Related to Tempo Cyclone Cyclone is a mobile code system being developed as part of the SwitchWare active-network project at the University of Pennsylvania. Cyclone uses two ideas to make mobile code safe as well as fast: run-time code generation and proof-carrying code. Cyclone relies on Tempo's analysis front-end (i.e. the binding-time analysis) and on TAL/T, an extension of the TAL typed assembly language. Workshop A workshop (actually closer to a ``winter school'') on Tempo has been organized at IRISA, March 16-18, 1998. The aim of this workshop was to present a three-day tutorial on Tempo and its applications to real size programs. We had 24 participants, coming from universities as well as industries. We believe it was a large success. The talks are now available on-line.

Depending on request, if the distribution of Tempo is a success, we might organize another workshop later. It would less be like a ``winter school'' but rather like a real workshop with users presenting applications and open discussions about possible improvements. It would be preceded by an optional one-day tutorial for people not knowing partial evaluation or Tempo.

Distribution The Tempo specializer has been made publicly available under a licence in April 1998. At of March 99, it was being used by about thirty people around the world. The binary version of Tempo has just (July 2000) been made available without any restrictions, and we expect a full unrestricted source release under GPL to follow soon.

Getting access to Tempo no longer requires signing a license agreement. Tempo is simply available via anonymous FTP, as described below. In any case, we would very much like to hear from you if you are an active Tempo user. If you are, please also let us know if and for what purpose you are using Tempo, by sending an email to tempo@labri.fr. We will by default add you to our tempo talk mailing list tempo-talk@labri.fr, where future Tempo releases will be announced, and Tempo users can discuss practical problems using Tempo.

Tempo can be downloaded :

Here is a Tempo release that have been made publicly available: i386 LinuxMost recent Tempo binary distribution for i386 Linux (tested on RedHat 6.1).(Please remember to send an email to tempo@labri.fr to let us know who you are and why you are using Tempo. Remember to explicitly indicate if you are not interested in joining the tempo-talk@labri.fr mailing list.)

In case of any problem with getting or installing the distribution, get in touch with us: mailto:tempo@labri.fr

References Here are general papers about Tempo and its architecture. More focused and up-to-date information regarding Tempo can be found in the main on-line papers tank. Revised version in Partial Evaluation, International Seminar, Dagstuhl Castle, LNCS 1110, Springer-Verlag, pages 54-72. [CHL+98] Tempo: Specializing Systems Applications and Beyond C. Consel, L. Hornof, J. Lawall, R. Marlet, G. Muller, J. Noyé, S. Thibault, N. Volanschi. To appear in ACM Computing Surveys, Symposium on Partial Evaluation, 1998. item.title: Yes, 17M lines of Lean is a lot
item.description:
Yes, 17m lines of Lean is a lot

The recent proof of the Riemann hypothesis came with a statistic attached: the proof is 17 million lines of Lean. Beyond the philosophical questions of what it means to have a proof longer than any human could comprehend, I’m left with a simpler question: is that as large as it sounds?

To investigate, I hunted for collections of Lean proofs online. I found two and charted the lengths of their proofs.

(All charts have a log x axis, which makes 17m lines look a lot closer to 1m and 100k than it really is.)

Famous theorems in Mathlib

Mathlib maintains a collection of famous proofs. There are over 1k but only 259 have Lean associated, which I chart here.

These are all human generated, and as we can see, they come nowhere close to 17m.

Every Lean package on Reservoir

Reservoir indexes every published Lean package, 938 of which have Lean code on GitHub. This one has a lot more data, including AI assisted proofs. We even have a few that are over 16m!:

88m: Qiuzhen-CFSG/CFSG this appears to be an AI built proof that is still a work in progress.

36m: CBirkbeck/LeanBridge, a project linking the LMFDB database of number theory objects to Mathlib. This isn’t really a proof: about 98% of its Lean is files generated by scripts that check the database’s numbers one by one. The hand-written part is closer to 500k lines.

27m: anthropics/fermats-last-theorem is another Anthropic special: a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, published on GitHub in September. Its README says “the Lean sources were produced by AI agents building on human-written open-source Lean”, including the human FLT project led by Kevin Buzzard, which is about 60k lines and still in progress. The AI version is roughly 450 times longer.

So yes, 17m lines is a lot.
